statements.text: Under a care perspective, rendering a person homeless is an extreme harm that normally outweighs the benefit of additional comfort to others when a less harmful alternative exists.
Eight-week uncompensated income loss is a serious but lesser harm than homelessness.
Providing cooling to heat-vulnerable households is an important caregiving good when it can be achieved without comparable or greater harms to others.
Plan A should be rejected because it imposes extreme harm (homelessness) on Mira.
Plan B is provisionally preferable among the three options under a care perspective.
Plan C should be rejected because it imposes serious economic harm on Sal while helping only one household and leaving others uncooled.
Compared with A, B avoids Mira's homelessness while still cooling many households.
Compared with C, B avoids Sal's income loss and cools more households, though it leaves Jo uncooled.

supports.explanation: Homelessness is an extreme harm to be avoided if possible.
B delivers care to 12 households without severe displacement or income loss.
C helps Jo but at disproportionate cost to Sal and other households.
Avoiding Mira's homelessness has priority over extra eight cooled homes.
Sal’s harm and uncooled households weigh more than Jo’s relief alone.

reasons.value: Provides cooling to many without severe harm
Serious income harm to Sal and fewer beneficiaries

comparisons.explanation: B spares Mira’s homelessness; extra heat for 8 is serious but lesser.
Switching to C helps Jo but harms Sal and 12 others; care priority keeps B.

conclusion: Under a care perspective that stresses preventing the gravest uncontrolled vulnerability, Plan B is the most defensible: it cools twelve households without rendering anyone homeless or stripping them of their entire income. Plan A is ruled out because it would leave Mira without housing, an extreme ongoing vulnerability. Plan C, while helping Jo, would strip Sal of all income for eight weeks and still leave twenty households without cooling, so it is less responsive overall than Plan B.
strongest_objection: Plan B leaves Jo—the single hottest residence—without cooling, ignoring a person in acute need.
answer_to_objection: Jo’s heat exposure is serious, but Plan C secures Jo’s relief only by imposing a new severe harm on Sal and neglecting twelve other households; Plan A still neglects Jo while making Mira homeless. Given present constraints, the care obligation to avoid the gravest newly created vulnerability (homelessness or total income loss) outweighs the benefit of targeting a single hottest home.
reversal_condition: If the council could guarantee Mira rehousing or compensate Sal fully, Plan A or C could become preferable because they would meet more or hotter households’ needs without leaving anyone in an extreme vulnerable state.
